chapter: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
title: Last seeing Jelly Roll Morton and how he dressed
summary: Howard recalls Morton walking into a 31st Street cafe where he was playing and remembers him as a sharp dresser.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Yes. When did you last see General Orton? By what? When did you last see General Orton? Oh boy. I don't remember that.

Yes I do. We were playing at a place on 31st Street. He wasn't playing though. I don't remember where he was playing at the time, but I remember him coming down there, I remember Ralph Emerson Brown playing saxophone. I was doubling on the fiddle and the clarinet. I don't remember who the piano player was, there was about five of us. This was you? This was? It wasn't my band, no. No, no. But we were playing in the Scheller Cafe that's at 31st Street, almost two blocks across the street from the Royal Gardens. Yes. And General Orton come in at that particular night. I don't know where he was working, I don't remember. But I don't remember what year it is to be truthful with you. That was a long time ago.
How old he dressed, do you remember?
I mean, why was he impressed he wasn't dressed so good?
I heard he was a very sharp dresser, was he?

He was, yeah. He dressed nice. He did. He did. He always looked nice in his clothes. I mean, he was built for it, he wasn't too heavy and tall. He could wear nice clothes. I mean, worrying somebody else would have to go to a tailor shop and, you know, be all old. I think he could just buy them, maybe little alterations and get away like that, because he was built like that. Built on Earl Hines is something like Earl.
